title: Adolescent well-being is diverging by gender and shaped across family, school, community, and digital environments
source_unit: OECD, Enhancing adolescent social and emotional well-being
geography: Cross-national OECD analysis of adolescent social and emotional well-being, gender differences, norms, and supportive environments

denominator.unit: adolescents aged 11-15 in the OECD Child Well-being Data Portal comparison

girls_poor_mental_wellbeing.unit: percent of girls aged 11-15 reporting poor mental well-being

boys_poor_mental_wellbeing.unit: percent of boys aged 11-15 reporting poor mental well-being

gender_gap.value: girls report substantially poorer mental well-being than boys across the OECD comparison

observations.method: OECD cross-national synthesis using the Child Well-being Data Portal and comparable adolescent self-reported social, emotional, and mental-well-being indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported well-being is sensitive to wording, culture, age, survey timing, and disclosure; cross-country differences do not identify a single cause or establish clinical diagnosis.
observations.subgroup: Adolescent girls and boys aged approximately 11-15, with attention to gender, age, social background, and differing forms of vulnerability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher reporting of distress can reflect greater recognition or willingness to disclose problems, while lower reporting does not establish better well-being or lower need.

observations.period: 2026; gendered patterns of social and emotional risk

denominator.unit: adolescent girls and boys across OECD comparative well-being evidence

girls_low_life_satisfaction.value: girls aged 11, 13, and 15 are between 1.65 and 2.5 times more likely than boys to report low life satisfaction

girls_internalising.value: girls face higher risks of anxiety, depression, body-image concerns, and self-harm

boys_externalising.value: boys face higher risks of conduct problems, aggression, and risk-taking; about one in seven adolescents report repeated physical fighting

observations.method: OECD synthesis of cross-national adolescent well-being, mental-health, behavior, and resilience measures, interpreted by age and sex.
observations.uncertainty: The indicators capture different constructs and sources; they are not interchangeable prevalence estimates for all mental-health conditions or explanations of gender differences.
observations.subgroup: Adolescent girls, boys, young people exposed to body-image or online pressures, and youth exhibiting internalising or externalising difficulties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Gender patterns are not fixed identities or universal experiences; class, disability, culture, family support, sexuality, race, and digital context can alter vulnerability and protection.

observations.period: 2026; social norms, identity, and adolescent behavior

norms.value: norms of femininity and masculinity can shape expectations, help-seeking, academic engagement, risk-taking, and self-image

digital_pressure.value: appearance pressures, social comparison, sexualisation, and online harms can intensify gendered well-being risks

help_seeking.value: restrictive masculinity norms can discourage help-seeking and contribute to disengagement or externalising behaviors

observations.method: OECD policy analysis linking adolescent outcomes to gender norms, family and school environments, community settings, and digital spaces.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies plausible social pathways but does not estimate the causal contribution of a specific norm, platform, household, or intervention.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents navigating identity formation, parents and caregivers, educators, peers, digital-platform users, and youth-serving institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Norms can provide structure and belonging as well as constraint; digital spaces can amplify harm but also support peer connection, information, and help-seeking.

denominator.unit: family, school, community, digital, and service environments shaping adolescent well-being

family_communication.value: around one-third of adolescents across the OECD report difficulties communicating with their parents

support_ecosystem.value: families, schools, communities, and digital environments all shape adolescent well-being and require coordinated support

service_boundary.value: specialist mental-health services are necessary but insufficient without prevention, school, family, community, and digital supports

observations.method: OECD synthesis of adolescent well-being indicators and policy evidence on prevention, early identification, family support, schools, communities, and online environments.
observations.uncertainty: The policy framework does not establish which combination of supports works best in every setting or how access and quality are distributed across groups.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents, parents and caregivers, schools, community organizations, mental-health providers, digital platforms, and public agencies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Single-sector services can be effective for particular needs; multi-sector coordination may also create referral burdens, privacy concerns, or uneven responsibility unless governance is clear.

related_sources.claim: OECD social-connections work provides complementary evidence on relationships, loneliness, and community conditions.
OECD trust-survey results provide complementary institutional and political-agency context.

boundary: This record adds an adolescent culture and well-being route linking gender norms, identity, family communication, school engagement, community space, digital environments, mental health, and public support systems. It uses publication-level cross-national aggregate and self-report evidence, not clinical records, respondent-level causal histories, platform trace data, or claims that any single environment causes an outcome.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD policy-paper page and full-report summaries were reviewed for gender differences, life satisfaction, mental well-being, norms, online harms, family communication, and multi-sector support claims.
